facts.text: The Moon makes no light of its own: it shines because sunlight hits it and reflects off its surface. The Sun lights the Moon from one side, so the half of the Moon facing the Sun is always lit and the half facing away is dark. Earth is lit the same way: the half facing the Sun has day, and the other half has night. Even at new moon, the Moon is still half lit; that lit half just faces away from Earth.

The Moon travels around Earth in a path called its orbit, so its position around Earth keeps changing. One full cycle of phases, from new moon back to new moon, takes about 29.5 days, roughly a month. The phases work like a classroom model: hold a ball at arm's length in a dark room lit by one lamp and turn slowly in a circle. The lamp always lights the half of the ball facing it, but as you turn you see more of that lit half, then less. The lamp stands for the Sun, the ball for the Moon, and your head for Earth, so the model shows every phase. Diagrams of the phases are not drawn to scale: the Sun is far bigger and much farther away than they show.

As the Moon moves along its orbit, we see different amounts of its lit half from Earth; these changing shapes are called phases, and the phase on any night shows where the Moon is in its orbit. The Moon itself does not change shape; only the part of its lit half that we see changes. At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so its lit half faces away and we see only its dark half: the Moon cannot be seen. About a week later, a quarter of the way around its orbit, comes first quarter, when half of the Moon's face looks lit and half looks dark. About two weeks after new moon, the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, with Earth between it and the Sun, so its whole lit half faces us: a full moon, a round disc. Then comes third quarter, three quarters of the way around, when half the face looks lit again, but on the opposite side from first quarter. While the lit part we see grows, from new moon to full moon, the Moon is waxing; while it shrinks, from full moon back to new moon, it is waning. Between new moon and the quarters the Moon looks like a thin crescent, and a few days after new moon a thin crescent can be seen low in the western sky just after sunset.

A common mistake is to think that Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases. In fact, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which can happen only at full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up exactly; most full moons have no eclipse, because the three usually do not line up exactly. Eclipses are usually the next topic after the phases. The same half-lit idea works the other way round: Earth is also half lit by the Sun, so someone standing on the Moon would see Earth go through phases, opposite to the Moon's phases. At new moon, the sunlit side of Earth faces the Moon and reflects sunlight toward it, so from the Moon Earth looks full: a round, shining, blue disc. At full moon, Earth's dark night side faces the Moon, so from the Moon Earth looks dark. As the Moon grows fuller in our sky, Earth seen from the Moon grows thinner.

misconception: A common mistake is thinking Earth's shadow causes the phases. Earth's shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse at some full moons; the phases come from seeing different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half.

lesson_markdown:
**Why does the Moon look like a thin sliver on some nights and a full, round circle on others?**

The Moon itself doesn't change shape. The Sun always lights half the Moon; as the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. These changing shapes are called **phases**.

## Try it with a lamp and a ball

Hold a ball at arm's length in a dark room lit by one lamp, then turn slowly in a circle. The lamp always lights the half of the ball facing it, but as you turn, you see more of that lit half, then less. The lamp stands for the Sun, the ball for the Moon, and your head for Earth.

## Why it happens

1. **The Moon makes no light of its own.** It shines because sunlight hits it and reflects off its surface.
2. **Half is always lit.** The Sun lights the Moon from one side, so the half facing the Sun is lit and the half facing away is dark.
3. **The Moon keeps moving.** It travels around Earth in a path called its **orbit**, so its position around Earth keeps changing.
4. **Our view changes.** As the Moon moves along its orbit, we see different amounts of its lit half from Earth.

You already know this idea from Earth itself: the half of Earth facing the Sun has day, and the other half has night.

## Four phases to know

Before the table, a question: where do you think the Moon has to be for us to see its whole lit half? It has to be on the far side of Earth from the Sun, so its whole lit half faces us.

| Phase | Where the Moon is | What we see |
|---|---|---|
| **New moon** | Between Earth and the Sun | Only the dark half, so the Moon can't be seen |
| **First quarter** | A quarter of the way around its orbit, about a week later | Half of the face lit, half dark |
| **Full moon** | On the far side of Earth from the Sun, about two weeks after new moon | The whole lit half: a round disc |
| **Third quarter** | Three quarters of the way around | Half of the face lit, on the opposite side from first quarter |

While the lit part we see grows, from new moon to full moon, the Moon is **waxing**. While it shrinks, from full moon back to new moon, it is **waning**. Between new moon and the quarters, it looks like a thin crescent. One full cycle takes about 29.5 days, roughly a month.

Here's a surprise: even at new moon, the Moon is still half lit. That lit half just faces away from us.

## A common mistake

A common mistake is to think that Earth's shadow causes the phases. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which can happen only at full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up exactly. Most full moons have no eclipse, so the phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see, not from a shadow.

*This is simplified:* diagrams of the phases are not drawn to scale. The Sun is far bigger and much farther away than they show.

## Check yourself

At first quarter, the Sun still lights a full half of the Moon. So why do we see only half of the Moon's face lit?

Curious how eclipses work, or what Earth looks like from the Moon? Ask a follow-up!

narration.text: Some evenings after sunset, a thin, curved sliver of Moon hangs low in the western sky.
Over the next few days it grows into half a circle, and later into a full, round disc.
Picture a dark room lit by a single lamp.
Hold out a ball, and the lamp lights only the half facing it.
Now turn slowly in a circle, and you see more of that lit half, then less.
The real Moon works the same way.
It makes no light of its own; it shines because light from the Sun reflects off it.
So the half facing the Sun is always lit, and the half facing away is dark.
At new moon, the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun.
Its lit half faces the Sun, so we face only its dark half and cannot see it.
Surprisingly, even at new moon the Moon is still half lit; that half just faces away from us.
The Moon travels around Earth along a path called its orbit, so its place around Earth keeps changing.
As it moves, more of the lit half turns toward us, and these changing shapes are called phases.
While the lit part we see is growing, we say the Moon is waxing.
About a week after new moon, it reaches first quarter, when half of its face looks lit.
So where must the Moon be for us to see its whole lit half?
It must be on the far side of Earth from the Sun, which gives us the full moon.
After that, the lit part we see shrinks, and we say the Moon is waning.
At third quarter, half of the face looks lit again, but on the opposite side from first quarter.
Then it slides back to new moon; one full cycle takes about twenty-nine and a half days.
A common mistake is to think that the shadow of Earth causes the phases.
That shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse, at a full moon when all three line up exactly.
Most full moons have no eclipse, so phases come from how much sunlit half we see.
The same idea works in reverse from the Moon.
At new moon, someone standing on the Moon would see a full, blue Earth, because the sunny side of Earth faces them.
At full moon, they would see the dark night side of Earth instead.
So remember this: the Sun always lights half the Moon; as the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.
The cause is the Moon moving around Earth; the result is a cycle of shapes about once a month.
Now the shape of the Moon on any night tells you where it is in its orbit.
